Religious Affections
ri-LIJ-uhs uh-FEK-shuhnz
theological work
From religious (pertaining to true worship and godliness) and affections (the inclinations and movements of the will); the title of Jonathan Edwards’s great treatise.

📖 Biblical Definition

A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections is Jonathan Edwards’s searching examination of the nature of true religion, written in the wake of the Great Awakening to distinguish the genuine work of the Spirit from its counterfeits. Edwards’s thesis is that “true religion, in great part, consists in holy affections”—that real godliness is not cold notional assent, nor mere outward duty, but the lively engagement of the heart, the will moved toward God in love, joy, hope, fear, and grief over sin. Yet Edwards is equally concerned to expose false affections: high feelings, fluent talk, abundant tears, and sudden raptures prove nothing in themselves, for hypocrites may have them all. He lays down distinguishing marks of gracious affections, chief among them their arising from the loveliness of divine things themselves, their tendency to humble the soul, and supremely their fruit in Christian practice—a holy life is the great evidence of a renewed heart. The dictionary commends the Affections as the finest anatomy of experimental religion in the English tongue, holding the narrow path between dead orthodoxy on the one hand and unbridled enthusiasm on the other. The heart must be engaged, but the test of the heart’s engagement is a transformed life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Jonathan Edwards’s classic treatise on the nature of true religion, holding that genuine godliness consists in holy affections proved by their fruit in a holy life.

RELIGIOUS AFFECTIONS, the title of Jonathan Edwards’s treatise on the nature of true religion.

Written after the Great Awakening to distinguish the Spirit’s work from its counterfeits.

Holds that true religion in great part consists in holy affections of the heart.

Exposes false affections—feelings, fluency, and raptures that prove nothing in themselves.

Names Christian practice, a holy life, as the chief sign of gracious affections.

Mat 7:20 — "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Edwards’s careful balance is broken on both sides—by dead orthodoxy that despises feeling, and by emotionalism that mistakes excitement for grace.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Edwards’s balance: true religion engages the affections, yet the test of those affections is not their intensity but their fruit in a holy life. Against the modern revival culture that measures God’s work by the height of feeling and the size of the response, Edwards insists that “the degree of religion is to be judged by the fixedness and strength of the habit that is exercised in affection, whereby holy affections are habitual.”

The corruption runs in two directions. On one side stands a dead orthodoxy that prides itself on doctrine while the heart lies cold, despising affection as mere emotionalism. On the other stands an unbridled enthusiasm that mistakes goosebumps and tears for regeneration and trusts a moment of high feeling as conversion. Edwards refutes both: the heart must truly be moved, but moved by the loveliness of God Himself, humbled rather than puffed up, and proved by a changed life. By their fruits ye shall know them.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The title joins true religion with the affections, the movements of the will, which Edwards held to be the seat of real godliness.

expand to see more

English affection — an inclination or vigorous movement of the will toward or against an object.

For Edwards the affections are “the more vigorous and sensible exercises of the inclination and will of the soul.”

Distinguished from mere passions or bodily emotions, though often attended by them.

Religious — pertaining to the true worship and service of God.

The title names the seat of true religion: not bare intellect, but the heart engaged toward God.

Usage

"Edwards’s Affections is the standard work cited in discerning true from false conversion."

"Its insistence on Christian practice as the chief sign is preached against easy-believism."

"The treatise is used to correct both cold orthodoxy and revivalist emotionalism."
